title: Earth Is Warming Nearly Twice as Fast as a Decade Ago, Scientists Confirm
excerpt: A landmark study finds global warming has accelerated to 0.35°C per decade since 2015, putting the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C threshold on track to be breached before 2030.
body:
• Global warming has accelerated from 0.2°C per decade to 0.35°C per decade since 2015, according to a study published in Geophysical Research Letters with over 98% statistical confidence.
  • If the current warming rate persists, the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C threshold could be breached between 2026 and 2029, researchers warn.
  • A separate report from 70+ international scientists found global greenhouse gas emissions hit an all-time high of 56.8 billion tonnes in 2024, with the remaining carbon budget likely exhausted within three years.
  • India faces outsized risks from accelerating warming, with monsoon disruptions, extreme heat events, and coastal flooding threatening hundreds of millions of lives and livelihoods.

For decades, climate scientists measured global warming at a relatively steady clip of about 0.2°C per decade. That era appears to be over. A peer-reviewed study published in Geophysical Research Letters by researchers at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research has established, with over 98% statistical confidence, that global warming is now accelerating — nearly doubling its pace to roughly 0.35°C per decade since 2015.

"We can now demonstrate a strong and statistically significant acceleration of global warming since around 2015," said Grant Foster, a retired statistician formerly at Tempo Analytics and co-author of the study. "The essential result of this paper isn't how fast we're warming, but that warming is now happening faster than before and that the difference isn't negligible."

Stripping Away the Noise

The breakthrough lies in the study's methodology. Lead author Stefan Rahmstorf and Foster analyzed five separate global temperature datasets — from NASA, NOAA, the UK Met Office, Berkeley Earth, and Copernicus ERA5 — after first removing the effects of natural climate fluctuations like El Niño, volcanic eruptions, and solar variation. Once that "noise" was stripped away, the acceleration became unmistakable across all five datasets.

The researchers pinpointed the shift to the 2013–2014 period. Before that, the planet had been warming at roughly 0.2°C per decade since the 1970s. After it, rates jumped to between 0.34°C and 0.42°C per decade depending on the dataset. Even after adjustment, 2023 and 2024 remain the two warmest years since instrumental records began in 1880.

"The adjusted data show an acceleration of global warming since 2015 with a statistical certainty of over 98%, consistent across all data sets examined and independent of the analysis method chosen."

— Stefan Rahmstorf, Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research

The 1.5°C Clock Is Ticking

The implications are stark. If the current warming rate holds, the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C threshold — widely regarded as the guardrail against catastrophic climate impacts — will be breached as a long-term average between 2026 and 2029, depending on the dataset used. Some estimates point to ERA5 data suggesting the breach could happen as early as this year.

A separate Indicators of Global Climate Change (IGCC) report, published in June 2026 by more than 70 scientists across 56 institutions, reinforced the urgency. It found that human-caused warming reached 1.37°C in 2025, with the remaining carbon budget — the total CO₂ that can still be emitted while staying below 1.5°C — estimated at just 130 gigatonnes from the start of 2026. At current emission rates of 56.8 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per year, that budget will be exhausted in roughly three years.

"A key indicator is the Earth's energy imbalance, which measures how fast heat is accumulating in the climate system," said Prof. Piers Forster, director of the Priestley Centre for Climate Futures at the University of Leeds. "Without human influence, it should be close to zero, but it has been growing since the 1970s and is now at a record high, doubling in recent decades."

Why Warming Is Speeding Up

The Rahmstorf-Foster study deliberately does not identify the causes of the acceleration, but other scientists have offered explanations. Dr. Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist contributing to Carbon Brief, pointed to reductions in sulfur dioxide emissions as the "most likely driver." Sulfur aerosols from burning fossil fuels have a cooling effect that partially masks greenhouse gas warming. As countries clean up air pollution — a health benefit — they inadvertently unmask decades of hidden warming.

The World Meteorological Organization added another layer of concern in May, forecasting an 86% chance that at least one year between 2026 and 2030 will surpass 2024 as the hottest on record. An El Niño event predicted for late 2026 could push 2027 into record territory.

Not all scientists agree on the precise pace. Prof. Michael Mann of the University of Pennsylvania has argued there is no evidence of acceleration beyond what decreased aerosols and El Niño explain. But even Mann acknowledges: "The planet is warming at a roughly constant rate and that's bad enough."

What This Means for India and the Diaspora

Accelerating global warming carries severe consequences for South Asia. India, home to 1.4 billion people, is among the nations most exposed to rising temperatures. The Indian Meteorological Department has recorded increasingly erratic monsoons, with both flooding and drought striking in the same season across different states. Extreme heat waves in 2024 and 2025 pushed temperatures above 50°C in parts of Rajasthan, and rising sea levels threaten Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata — cities where millions live near the coast.

For the Indian diaspora, the stakes are both personal and economic. Remittances to India — the largest in the world at over $125 billion annually — flow to families in climate-vulnerable regions. Agricultural disruptions, water scarcity, and health impacts from heat stress ripple through communities that many abroad still call home.

What's Next

The Rahmstorf-Foster study's authors caution that whether warming continues to accelerate depends entirely on how fast the world cuts fossil fuel emissions to zero. Dr. Claudie Beaulieu of the University of California praised the study but stressed that "the acceleration may prove temporary" and that "continued monitoring over the next several years will be essential."

With the remaining carbon budget measured in months rather than decades, the window for action is narrowing faster than most climate models predicted even five years ago. The question is no longer whether warming is accelerating — it is whether the world can decelerate emissions fast enough to matter.
